To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The Parkin co-regulator gene (PACRG) is required for normal cilia function and is a candidate gene for ciliopathies such as hydrocephalus (2) PACRG is a novel regulator of the ciliary motor apparatus, and its loss results in reduced cilial beating (3) Transgenic expression of PacRG rescues the hydrocephalus phenotype in the qv viable mutant mouse.
the deletion of the Pacrg gene causes defects in ciliary motility in the ependymal cells and leads to the development of acquired, communicating hydro-cephalus in the Qkv mutant mouse.

the Parkin co- regulated gene (PACRG) is necessary and sufficient for the function of ependyma cilia and the development of hydrocephalus (a ciliopathy) in the mouse model of the qkv (quaking viable) mutant mouse.

the molecular basis of inherited neurological diseases and the development of new therapies for these diseases.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that Pacrg is essential for the proper function of cilia in the mouse brain and that its loss causes hydrocephalus.
Pacrg is a ciliary protein and that it is required for the normal function of ependyma cilia.
the Parkin co regulated gene (PACRG) is a ciliopathy gene.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Pacrg protein is required for proper motility of the ependymal cells, which line the ventricles of the brain and generate the flow of cerebrospinal fluid.
Pacrg is essential for motile ciliary function in vivo.
the Parkin-co-regulated gene is a critical regulator of ciliary beat frequency and is required for the maintenance of ependyma in the central canal of the spinal cord.
